titulo: Toxic and Non-toxic Plants: Peace Lily
texto:
Toxicity for dogs and cats
Additional Common Names: Mauna Loa Peace Lily. Scientific Name: Spathiphyllum. Family: Araceae.

Toxicity: Toxic to Dogs, Toxic to Cats.

Toxic Principles: Insoluble calcium oxalates.

Clinical Signs: Oral irritation, intense burning and irritation of mouth, tongue and lips, excessive drooling, vomiting, difficulty swallowing.

If you suspect your pet may have ingested a potentially toxic substance, call the ASPCA Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 or contact your local veterinarian as soon as possible.

titulo: Assessing biochar, clinoptilolite zeolite and zeo-char loaded nano-nitrogen for boosting growth performance and biochemical ingredients of peace lily (Spathiphyllum wallisii) plant under water shortage
texto:
Abstract: background and conclusion
Peace lily (Spathiphyllum wallisii Regel) is an ornamental indoor plant with promising cut flower market, as well as antiviral, pharmacological and ecological potentials. Water deficiency can have sound effects on the growth performance and aesthetic quality of such plant. The aim of this study was to investigate the consequences of zeolite, biochar, and zeo-char loaded nano-nitrogen application on the growth performance and biochemical components of peace lily under water shortage conditions. An experiment was conducted over two consecutive seasons (2021–2022) at the experimental nursery of Ornamental Horticulture Department, Faculty of Agriculture, Cairo University, Giza, Egypt.

Antioxidant enzymes (catalase and peroxidase), proline and abscisic acid (ABA) exhibited significant declines with zeo-char loaded nano-N treatment relative to control. These findings suggest that incorporating soil amendments with nano-nutrients could provide a promising approach towards improving growth performance and quality of ornamental, medicinal and aromatic species under water deficiency conditions.

titulo: Assessing biochar, clinoptilolite zeolite and zeo-char loaded nano-nitrogen for boosting growth performance and biochemical ingredients of peace lily (Spathiphyllum wallisii) plant under water shortage
texto:
Water stress in ornamental plants
Spathiphyllum wallisii Regel or peace lily, a member of Araceae, is a shade tolerant indoor ornamental plant species with little water needs.

Water deficiency or water shortage could affect the aesthetic value of ornamental plants and decrease their marketability due to its effect on their most wanted features; leaves and flowers. Declination of leaf parameters (number, area, and color intensity) and flower characters (number and turnover) in response to water stress conditions were reported by several authors. The reduction in growth parameters is associated with physiological and biochemical changes; some of which are adaptive mechanisms to cope with stress and improve plant performance. For example, reduced leaf size and area is one of these mechanisms in which plant aims to reduce stress by decreasing surface area subjected to water loss.

Moreover, increment in abscisic acid (ABA) in response to water stress will stimulate stomatal closure, which in turn, will decrease stomatal conductance, photosynthetic activity and CO2 assimilation. Although these mechanisms are directed towards the efficient use of available water and alleviating stress conditions, however, reduction of photosynthetic rate and CO2 assimilation will negatively affect the overall plant growth performance. Moreover, prolonged water stress could lead to oxidative stress resulting from the excessive production of reactive oxygen species (ROS). Increment in free proline content also is an important defense mechanism against stress conditions, where proline is an important osmolyte functioning to restore osmotic potential and consequently cell membrane integrity and homeostasis.

titulo: Assessing biochar, clinoptilolite zeolite and zeo-char loaded nano-nitrogen for boosting growth performance and biochemical ingredients of peace lily (Spathiphyllum wallisii) plant under water shortage
texto:
Turgor loss and growth under water deficit
Reductions in growth parameters are direct results of soil water limitation on plant performance due to scarce water availability to plants, which limits water movement and hydraulic conductivity within roots, hence reducing nutrient transport –especially of N- required for plant growth, which in turn affects cell division and elongation. Loss of cell turgor due to declination of osmotic potential caused by water stress also has a negative impact on plant growth parameters such as root length and plant biomass. Other responses could be adaptive mechanisms to cope with stress consequences such as reduction in leaf size and area to reduce water loss through transpiration, hence improving water use efficiency. Such reduction in leaf parameters of ornamental plants could affect their aesthetic value and decrease their marketability.

In the current research, declined growth parameters for control plants of peace lily subjected to water limitation with only recommended chemical NPK supplementation matches well with the previous literature.

titulo: Assessing biochar, clinoptilolite zeolite and zeo-char loaded nano-nitrogen for boosting growth performance and biochemical ingredients of peace lily (Spathiphyllum wallisii) plant under water shortage
texto:
Phytohormones, antioxidant enzymes and proline
Activity of enzymatic antioxidants (CAT and POD), ABA and proline contents are raised in peace lily plants in response to water deficit; NPK supply only was not able to improve stress status. While increased CAT and POD activities are important tolerance mechanisms to alleviate oxidative stress by ROS scavenging, increased proline acts to adjust osmotic pressure and restore cell turgor under water deficit conditions. Moreover, production of ABA in roots increase in water stress conditions and is transferred to leaves to enhance stomatal closure in order to reduce transpiration and preserve water content necessary for keeping photosynthetic function. On the other hand, GA3 content is reduced under water deficit conditions.

Conclusion
Water deficiency majorly affects growth performance and quality of peace lily plants in an adverse manner. In that concern, control plants subjected to water deficit with the application of inorganic NPK showed significant lower values for all vegetative and anatomical parameters, macro- and micronutrients contents, biochemical components (total chlorophyll, total carotenoids, total carbohydrates, total phenolic compounds, total flavonoids, and tannins) and GA3. Some parameters such as antioxidant enzymes (CAT and POD), ABA, and proline were significantly higher in case of control plants; these act usually as adaptive tolerance mechanisms against water stress. Significant decreases were notable for antioxidant enzymes, ABA and proline with the soil amendments; such decrements indicate that plants were able to regain cell turgor and homeostasis and counteract stress conditions.

titulo: Spathiphyllum (Peace Lily, Spathe Flower, White Sails)
texto:
Description
Peace lily is a group of about 60 species of flowering plants that are semi-evergreen, perennial herbs typically grown as houseplants. They are members of the arum family (Araceae) and are native to Mexico, tropical America, Malesia and islands of the western Pacific. The genus name is Greek for "spathe leaf," referring to the prominent spathe, which is a modified leaf.

While peace lilies can grow up to 6 feet tall, they more typically reach 3 feet high and wide in an indoor setting. Dwarf cultivars are available. The plants have no specific bloom time, but flower freely. These low-maintenance plants are popular as specimens or accents in interior groupings for their deep-green glossy foliage and showy, white blooms that change to pale green after 10 days and then remain lovely for at least another month.

Light, temperature, water and fertilizer
Peace lilies prefer partial to deep shade. Do not place plants in direct sun. They enjoy warm conditions between 68 and 85 degrees F during the day and no more than a 10-degree drop at night. Cold and drafty conditions, specifically temperatures of 40 to 60 degrees F, will slow growth considerably. Extended periods below 40 degrees F can damage leaves, stems and roots.

Keep the soil moist, but not soggy; allow it to dry between waterings. Watering from below works very well for peace lilies. Fertilize at one-quarter of the recommended strength and flush soil between applications of fertilizer. Over-fertilizing and salt build-up can burn the leaf tips and roots. The plant requires a large pot and should be kept somewhat pot-bound. Use a potting mix high in organic matter. Re-pot, when necessary, in February or March.

Cultural conditions: Light: deep shade (less than 2 hours to no direct sunlight) or partial shade. Soil texture: high organic matter. Soil pH: acid (<6.0). Soil drainage: good drainage, moist. USDA Plant Hardiness Zone: 11a, 11b, 12a, 12b. Recommended propagation strategy: division.

titulo: Spathiphyllum (Peace Lily, Spathe Flower, White Sails)
texto:
Insects, Diseases and Other Plant Problems
Mealybugs are probably the most common insect indoors. Because of the wide foliage, cleaning the leaves regularly with a damp cloth to remove dust will help its appearance and remove some pests that tend to gather under the bottom of the leaves. Brown leaf tips are caused by excessive direct sunlight, underwatering, or low humidity. Spathiphyllum has some other problems: purple mite.

Poisonous to Humans and Pets
This plant has medium severity poison characteristics. Problems: poisonous to humans; problem for cats, children, dogs and horses.

Poison symptoms: The leaves of the Peace Lily can be poisonous if eaten in large quantities. Symptoms include severe pain in the mouth and a burning sensation to the lips, tongue, and throat, excessive drooling, vomiting (not horses), difficulty swallowing. Poison toxic principle: calcium oxalate crystals. Poison part: leaves.

titulo: How to grow peace lilies — RHS Growing Guide
texto:
Quick Facts
Popular, low-maintenance houseplants. These tropical plants like warmth, humid air and indirect light. Water regularly but moderately, letting the compost dry out each time.

What are peace lilies?
These evergreen plants come from tropical forests in Central America and Colombia, so need warmth and indirect or filtered light. They prefer moderate humidity too, and regular watering through the growing season.

Although known as peace lilies, they aren't related to lilies, but instead belong to the arum family (Araceae) and have the typical arum 'flower', comprising a large petal-like spathe, surrounding a spike, or spadix, which holds the tiny true flowers. The spathes resemble white flags, a symbol of peace, which is the origin of the plant's common name. They are mainly produced in spring and summer, lasting for several months before fading to green.

Take care: Peace lilies, like many of their fellow arums, are poisonous, so wear gloves when handling them and position them out of reach of children and pets.

titulo: How to grow peace lilies — RHS Growing Guide
texto:
Planting
Newly purchased peace lilies can usually stay in their original container for at least a year or two before repotting is required. Then in spring, at the beginning of the growing season, check the roots by removing the pot – plants only need repotting when the roots are densely packed.

To repot, select peat-free multi-purpose compost and mix in perlite to improve the drainage – ideally at a 3:1 ratio. The new pot should be only a few centimetres larger than the current one, to avoid overpotting. Using a much larger pot can mean the excess compost stays damp for too long, potentially leading to root rot.

Location
Keep peace lilies in bright, indirect light – near a window but not in direct summer sun – to ensure strong growth and flowering. Plants will survive in deeper shade but will rarely flower and will grow very slowly.

Average room temperatures are fine, anywhere between 12–24°C (55–75°F), but keep plants away from hot radiators and cold draughts.

titulo: How to grow peace lilies — RHS Growing Guide
texto:
Watering
Water peace lilies throughout the growing season, from April to October, once the top few centimetres of compost have become dry. Reduce watering slightly in winter when growth slows down. The fluoride in tap water can damage the foliage, so use rainwater or filtered water whenever possible.

If the compost dries out very quickly after watering, this may be a sign that your plant is rootbound and in need of a larger pot. Repot it in spring.

Each time you water your peace lily, turn the pot by a quarter, to prevent it growing towards the light and becoming lop-sided.

Humidity
Peace lilies prefer moderate humidity – their leaves may start to turn brown if the air is too dry. So stand the pot in a saucer over a tray of damp gravel – the water will slowly evaporate, raising the humidity around the plant.

Glossary note (RHS): If air humidity is low, plants transpire quickly and become at risk of wilting if water is lost from the leaves faster than it can be absorbed by the roots.

titulo: How to grow peace lilies — RHS Growing Guide
texto:
Feeding, pruning and propagating
To boost leaf production and flowering, apply a general liquid fertiliser every few weeks throughout the growing season, from April to October.

Simply snip off any fading leaves and spent flowers at the base of the stem. Wear gloves, as the sap can be a skin irritant.

The easiest way to propagate peace lilies is by dividing a large, established clump in spring. Remove the plant from its pot then cut or pull apart the rootball to create several smaller plants, each with plenty of roots and several strong stems. Pot them up individually into free-draining peat-free compost.

Problems
Peace lilies are generally healthy, tolerant and trouble-free, but bear in mind the following:

- Keeping the compost too wet for long periods can result in root rot. Let the top of the compost dry out between waterings, and reduce watering in winter. Overwatering can also cause browning or yellowing leaves.
- Lack of water can cause peace lilies to droop alarmingly, but if you water them promptly, they should soon recover with no ill-effects.
- Dry air can result in leaves turning brown at the edges – so mist plants regularly and stand the pot in a tray of damp gravel to increase humidity.
- Failure to flower is often due to insufficient light – position near a window in bright light, but out of direct summer sun.

Peace lilies
Peace lilies (Spathiphyllum wallisii) are popular houseplants with distinctive white flower-like spathes that stand above the glossy tropical foliage. Easy to grow and happy in indirect light, they make elegant additions to any home.

Appearance
Peace lilies form a clump of glossy dark green leaves, 30–60cm (1–2ft) tall. Their 'flowers' comprise a flamboyant white petal-like spathe that surrounds a central cream-coloured spike (spadix). These stand above the leaves to create a striking display that lasts for several months. The spathes turn greener as they age.

Preferences
They like consistent warmth and moderate humidity – a bathroom is an ideal location for them. They prefer rainwater to tap water. Wipe the leaves with a damp cloth to remove dust and improve photosynthesis.

Dislikes
Very dry air can cause leaf browning – mist plants regularly or stand them on a tray of damp gravel, and keep them away from hot radiators and cold draughts. The roots can rot if the compost is damp for long periods, so take care not to overwater. Direct summer sunshine can scorch the foliage. Plants can droop dramatically when they need watering, but soon perk up after a good drink.

Did you know?
Peace lilies are members of the arum family and, like many of their relatives, are poisonous, so keep them out of reach of children and pets. Also wear gloves when handling them, as the sap can cause skin irritation.

titulo: Chilling Injury in Tropical Foliage Plants: I. Spathiphyllum (ENH841)
texto:
Chilling temperatures
The genus Spathiphyllum, commonly known as Peace Lily, has about 36 species. Most species originate in Central and South America, but two have their native habitat in the Malay Archipelago. Because of their elegant white spathes, deep green foliage, and ability to tolerate low light, Peace Lily has become one of the most popular ornamental foliage plants.

Spathiphyllum, like most other foliage plants with tropical origin, is sensitive to chilling temperatures. A chilling temperature can be any temperature that is cold enough to cause injury but not cold enough to freeze the plant, usually ranging from just above 32°F to 59°F. Chilling injury has been a significant cause of losses in foliage plant production, transportation, and interiorscaping.

Chilling Injury Symptoms
Chilling injury initiated from leaf tips and edges and progressed inwardly, with injured leaf areas becoming necrotic, then turning black, and, finally, drying up completely. Symptoms appeared within 24 hours for 'Mini' and 5 days for '5598' after initial exposure to 38°F. Degree of the visual injury ranged from minor necrotic lesions on leaf tips or edges to the complete death of plants, depending on cultivars, when exposed to 38°F.

In general, mature leaves were more sensitive to chilling than young leaves. Prolonged exposure to either 38°F or 45°F caused more injury than a shorter period of exposure at these temperatures, and injury was more pronounced at 38°F than at 45°F. Therefore, chilling injury can be lessened if preventative actions are taken to reduce either the severity or the duration of chilling, or both.

No visual injury occurred in plants exposed to 52°F. However, when growth indices were measured 45 days after chilling, they were found to be smaller than those of the controls, suggesting that plant growth was actually affected by chilling exposure. This could explain why some cultivars recover slowly in spring even when temperature becomes optimal and nutrient supply is adequate.

titulo: Chilling Injury in Tropical Foliage Plants: I. Spathiphyllum (ENH841)
texto:
Summary
Compared to Aglaonema cultivars, which are often visibly injured at 50°F, Spathiphyllum cultivars indeed appear to be more resistant to chilling temperatures. Growers, however, should be particularly aware of the invisible effect of chilling in Spathiphyllum, which may be wrongly diagnosed as insufficient fertilization or other culture practices.

In summary, chilling injury in Spathiphyllum can be either visible or invisible. Visible injury ranging from necrotic lesions to complete plant death occurred when plants were exposed to 38°F or 45°F for 5 days. The reduction or delay in plant growth mainly reflects invisible injury when Spathiphyllum is exposed to 50°F. Cultivars differ significantly in resistance to chilling.

Peace Lily
Peace lilies, or spathiphyllums, are a popular indoor plant because of their beauty and hardy nature. They are easy to grow and can provide years of enjoyment. Peace lilies have large, dark green leaves and showy, spoon-shaped, white flowers and grow from one to four feet tall.

Keep your peace lily in a well-lit area, but out of direct sunlight. They do like damp soil, but avoid over-watering. The leaves may get dusty, and can be easily cleaned by wiping with a soft, damp cloth. Propagate your peace lily by division in the spring.

Research has shown that indoor plants, like peace lilies, help to clean the air indoors, and can improve mood and work productivity.

titulo: Florida Foliage House Plant Care: Spathiphyllum (ENH1216)
texto:
Introduction
Most Spathiphyllum are seen in flower when at market. The attractive white blooms, called spathes, are long lasting. With proper plant care, Spathiphyllum may produce blooms year after year. Spathiphyllum is a very attractive house plant even when not in bloom and adapts well to home and patio environments.

Common names: Spathiphyllum, peace lily. Scientific name: Spathiphyllum spp. Plant family: Araceae (the aroid family).

Indoor/Home/Office Cultivation Information
- Light requirement: Bright, indirect light. No direct sun.
- Soil preference: Rich, organic peat or bark-based, bagged potting soil.
- Water requirement: Keep moist, but do not allow Spathiphyllum to sit in water.
- Drought tolerant: Slightly tolerant.
- Fertilizer requirements: Apply a low dose of liquid fertilizer according to manufacturer instructions three times per year.
- Salt tolerant: No.
- Temperature preference: Warm, tropical, 75°F–85°F.
- Chill tolerant (55°F–35°F): Moderately tolerant; some cultivars can be injured at 35°F; active growth is reduced at or below 50°F.
- Freeze tolerant (below 32°F): No.
- Pests: Mealybug, scale. Take a sample to your local UF/IFAS Extension agent to confirm identification and receive treatment instructions.

Outdoor Cultivation Information
- Outdoor year-round planting: Okay for USDA Hardiness Zones 10B–12.
- Soil preference: Well drained, amended with organic matter.
- Light requirement: No direct sun.
- Water requirement: Irrigate regularly; maintain moisture but provide drainage.
- Drought tolerant: Slightly tolerant.
- Fertilizer requirements: Apply a well-balanced, slow-release, pelletized fertilizer according to manufacturer recommendations during the warm growing season.
- Temperature preference: Warm, tropical 75°F–85°F.
- Pests: Mites, scale.

Notes: Spathiphyllum varieties are numerous and range in size from small plants in 4-inch pots to specimen sizes in 7-gallon pots or larger.

titulo: Cultural Guidelines for Commercial Production of Interiorscape Spathiphyllum (ENH958)
texto:
Origin and description
Spathiphyllum literally translates into "leaf spathe." It is commonly called Peace Lily, Snowflower, Spathe Flower, or White Anthurium. Spathiphyllum belongs to the family Araceae, has about 41 species, and originates from Panama, Columbia, Ecuador, Venezuela, the Malay Archipelago, Costa Rica, and the Philippines where it thrives in humid, tropical rainforest understories.

Peace Lily is an herbaceous evergreen with short, erect to creeping stems bearing tufts of foliage. Leaves are dark green and ovate to lanceolate. The inflorescence is a white, hood-shaped spathe sheltering a cream/white spadix covered with bisexual flowers. From an ornamental viewpoint, the spathes and spadices are called flowers rather than the tiny true flowers on the spadix. Inflorescences are produced seasonally or intermittently and can also be induced with chemical sprays.

Spathiphyllum cultivars are popular interiorscape plants in part because of the wide selection of cultivars ranging in height from 12 inches to 4 feet. Also, they are easy to care for and they are attractive plants, with dark green foliage contrasting with lily-white flowers. NASA even praised them in the Clean Air Study for their ability to remove formaldehyde, benzene, and carbon monoxide from interior air.

titulo: Cultural Guidelines for Commercial Production of Interiorscape Spathiphyllum (ENH958)
texto:
Production: substrate, light and fertilizer
Peace Lily requires container substrates possessing high water and nutrient holding capacities. Canadian peat at 50 to 60% in volume is often combined with pine bark, vermiculite, or coir as the container substrate for Spathiphyllum production. Plants should be grown under 1500-2500 fc, which is about 75% shade in winter and 80% in summer in Florida. Excessive light bleaches leaves and the resulting pale color is often misidentified as a nutrient deficiency.

Fertilizer rates vary according to temperature. If foliar sprays are used, they are best applied to the underside of the leaf since the upper side is waxy, and the spray will leave a gray residue. Growers are recommended to monitor media soluble salts and pH every 2 or 3 weeks using the pour-through method. Spathiphyllum has rather thin but abundant leaves; keep container substrates moist during periods when temperatures exceed 80°F.

Production: temperature and flowering
A general consensus among growers is that Spathiphyllum is more cold tolerant than other aroids. Our studies showed that exposure to 45°F could cause chilling injury in some cultivars, and delayed or reduced growth occurred when plants were exposed to 52°F for five days. The preferred temperature range for Peace Lily production is 70-90°F.

The market value of Spathiphyllum depends heavily on the presence of flowers. Most Spathiphyllum cultivars only flower from January to August. In order to have a year-round flowering, a foliar spray of gibberellic acid (GA3) at a concentration of 250 ppm has been widely used in flower induction. Depending on cultivars, flowers will appear in 9 to 12 weeks after GA3 spray.

titulo: Cultural Guidelines for Commercial Production of Interiorscape Spathiphyllum (ENH958)
texto:
Shipping and Interior Care
Use sleeves when shipping to avoid damage to the thin leaves. Shipping temperatures can range from 55 to 60°F. Once placed in interior conditions, individual blooms may last for a month or so. Trim dead blooms and leaves as soon as possible. Avoid over-fertilizing, as high soluble salts will burn leaf tips and margins. Using a 20-20-20 water soluble fertilizer solution with a N level at 50 ppm once a month or maintaining a soluble salts range of 0.8 to 1.2 dS/m should be adequate under interior conditions. The most common problem is underwatering which causes the entire plant to severely wilt or, as it is known in the trade, "crash."

Another maintenance problem with Spathiphyllum is a tendency to accumulate dust on their leaves. Wipe with a damp cloth to remove dust and the occasional pest. An occasional light spray of leaf polish is also recommended to reduce dust accumulation.

titulo: Cultural Guidelines for Commercial Production of Interiorscape Spathiphyllum (ENH958)
texto:
Physiological problems: water
Symptom: Leaves wilt or collapse and sometimes develop necrosis along leaf margins. Roots are sparse, sometimes with black tips. Probable cause: Saturated soil medium. Treatment: Reduce irrigation frequency to improve soil aeration or utilize a potting medium with a higher pore space percentage. This is more likely to occur during cold weather when the plant's watering needs decrease.

Symptom: "Crashing" or wilting so severely that the plant droops to soil level. Probable cause: Lack of water. Treatment: Simple and thorough watering is sufficient. Plants will resurrect in a matter of hours. Some damage may occur in the form of chlorosis and/or necrosis once the plant turgor is restored. Plants may droop in the late day if they are in bright light and temperatures are above 80-85°F even though potting mix is moist. This is normal. However, frequent drooping will result in brown tips and edges.

Physiological problems: nutrition, light and cold
Symptom: Reduced growth and chlorotic leaves. This disorder frequently occurs during winter months when soil is cold. Probable cause: Nutrient deficiency. Treatment: Foliar sprays are beneficial. Usually iron or manganese sprays are best. Magnesium additives are needed if chlorosis is only on the lower leaf margins.

Symptom: Leaves may be curled, pale, and chlorotic to necrotic. Often leaves have burned margins and tips, and flowering is sparse. Probable cause: Excess light or temperature. Treatment: Reduce the light level to 2500 foot-candles or below and/or the temperature to 90°F (32.2°C) or lower. These plants will sunburn. If this is the case, remove the plant from direct sunlight.

Symptom: Lack of flowering especially with young plants. Probable cause: Plants are immature. Plants grown for 9 to 15 months will usually bloom between February and April, depending on winter growing temperatures.

Symptom: Burnt tips and roots. Probable cause: Excessive fertilizer. Treatment: Interior plants require less fertilizer than greenhouse plants. Therefore, adjust fertilizer regime to ¼ strength suggested for commercial growers. Leaching prior to reducing fertilizer helps to eliminate this problem.

Symptom: Stunted growth, black areas on leaves and death of some roots. Injury usually begins at leaf tips and progresses inward with necrosis. Mature leaves are more sensitive than new leaves. Probable cause: Cold and drafts or extended periods below 45°F (7.2°C). Treatment: Keep daytime temperatures between 68 and 85°F (20 and 29.4°C) with a 5°F drop at night.

titulo: Cómo decide el semáforo: la regla sonda + riego
texto:
La regla vigente
El modelo final de la Tarea 2 se llama `regla-p3-f07-79b556`. Es una regla de cuatro pasos, que se aplica en este orden:

| condición | clase del modelo | cómo está Ruperto | LED |
|---|---|---|---|
| pasaron 5,5 h o menos desde el último riego | `estresada` | estresado, recuperándose del riego | amarillo |
| `suelo_mv` ≤ 1716 mV | `saludable` | saludable | verde |
| `suelo_mv` ≤ 1940 mV | `estresada` | estresado | amarillo |
| si no (más de 1940 mV) | `marchita` | marchito | rojo |

Las clases del modelo (`saludable`, `estresada`, `marchita`) son nombres internos del firmware y de los datos; Ruperto, que es varón, dice "estresado" y "marchito".

Se exporta como un árbol de decisión de 7 nodos que ocupa 111 bytes en la placa y decide con a lo sumo 3 comparaciones, en menos de un microsegundo. La predicción se calcula en la placa cada 5 minutos y no depende del WiFi.

titulo: Cómo decide el semáforo: la regla sonda + riego
texto:
Cómo se detecta un riego
Las "horas desde el riego" (`h_desde_riego`) se calculan así: si la sonda cae **250 mV o más** entre dos muestras seguidas, con una lectura real (no repetida) y con al menos una hora de historia en la ventana (fuera del warm-up tras un arranque), se guarda la hora de esa muestra como último riego. La placa la guarda en su memoria permanente, así que un reinicio no la olvida. Si no hubo riego o fue hace más de 96 horas, vale 96.

La regla del riego existe porque, después de regar, el sustrato se moja en minutos pero Ruperto tarda horas en recuperar la turgencia: durante esas horas sigue estresado (clase `estresada`) aunque la sonda ya diga húmedo.

Cuánto acierta
Se evaluó partiendo por episodios de etiqueta (no por filas, porque las muestras contiguas están correlacionadas y un split aleatorio da ~98 % por pura fuga). Con 20 episodios sin los dudosos:

- **F1 macro 0,858 ± 0,049**, exactitud balanceada 0,860, recall de `marchita` 0,77.
- Le gana a la regla de dos umbrales sobre la sonda sola en el 98 % de las remuestras por episodio, y a un árbol de decisión en el 99 %.
- Con todos los episodios, incluidos los dudosos, el F1 macro baja a 0,795.
- Ninguna `saludable` se confunde con `marchita` ni al revés: los errores son entre clases vecinas.

Se compararon once modelos (árbol, regresión logística, random forest, k-NN, SVM, MLP, naive Bayes y baselines). La regla quedó primera y es además de las más baratas.

titulo: Cómo decide el semáforo: la regla sonda + riego
texto:
Qué variables usa y cuáles no
Usa sólo la sonda de suelo y las horas desde el riego. La humedad del aire ayudaba un poco dentro de un árbol, pero ese aporte salía de los días sobre el radiador de septiembre. La **luz quedó afuera** a propósito: el modelo aprendía la hora en que el observador miraba la planta, no la planta. La hora del día tampoco entra por la misma razón.

Qué modelo corre hoy en la placa
Al 2026-11-03 la placa corre el **firmware 2.0.0 con un modelo viejo** (`arbol-p2-f012-58e644`, un árbol de sonda + temperatura). El firmware 2.1.0 con la regla final nunca se flasheó. Por eso la predicción que llega desde la placa puede no coincidir con la regla vigente; el bot recalcula la regla en el servidor y, si no coinciden, lo dice.

Historia de versiones
`arbol-p2-f012-58e644` (21/10, 11 episodios, sonda + temperatura) → `arbol-p3-f03-ee3419` (23/10, sonda + humedad del aire, F1 0,711) → `regla-p3-f07-79b556` (23/10, sonda + riego, F1 0,858).

titulo: Cómo se registraron los datos y las etiquetas
texto:
Muestreo
La placa mide cada 5 minutos (en septiembre y principios de octubre, con un firmware viejo, mandaba cada 30 segundos; para analizar se agrupa todo en intervalos de 5 minutos con la mediana). Cada muestra viaja con la hora de la placa en UTC, el valor crudo del ADC además del convertido, un número de muestra correlativo y un identificador de arranque (`boot_id`) que cambia en cada reinicio.

Episodios de etiqueta
La etiqueta no se guarda fila por fila sino como **episodios**: intervalos de tiempo durante los cuales la planta estuvo en un estado (`saludable`, `estresada` o `marchita`). Están en `data/episodios.csv`, con una nota que explica cada uno. Cada episodio tiene un origen:

- `manual`: alguien miró la planta y apretó el botón dentro del episodio. Es la única evidencia directa.
- `propagada`: la placa arrancó con la etiqueta anterior guardada y la siguió mandando; nadie miró.
- `corregida`: se reconstruyó después, de memoria o con fotos.

titulo: Cómo se registraron los datos y las etiquetas
texto:
Etapas del registro
- **12 al 17/09**: primeras mediciones. El 15 y el 16/09 la maceta estuvo sobre un radiador (hasta 35,6 °C y ~23 % de humedad del aire, la condición más exigente de todo el registro).
- **17/09 al 01/10**: hueco de dos semanas sin datos.
- **01 al 03/10**: episodios 8 a 10.
- **03 al 18/10**: tres ciclos casi iguales de unos 5 días: saludable → estresado (el sustrato se seca) → marchito (unas 12 h, de día) → riego a las 18:00 UTC → estresado unas 5–6 h de recuperación → saludable. Ambiente estable: 18,5–21,3 °C y 44–55 % de humedad del aire.
- **18 al 22/10**: episodios 11 a 15, con el marchitamiento nocturno del 19/10 y el riego de ese día a las 22:41 UTC.
- **22/10**: se flasheó el firmware 2.0.0 (con el modelo en la placa).
- **Hasta el 29/10 21:12 UTC**: última muestra recibida.

Riegos detectados en el entrenamiento
Con la regla de la caída de 250 mV, los riegos detectados en los datos de entrenamiento fueron el **07/10 18:00, 12/10 18:00, 17/10 18:00 y 19/10 22:40** (hora UTC; en Montevideo son tres horas menos).

Hora local
Los datos se guardan en UTC. Montevideo está en UTC−3 todo el año (Uruguay no usa horario de verano), así que un riego a las 18:00 UTC fue a las 15:00 en Montevideo.

titulo: Lo que Ruperto no sabe: limitaciones conocidas
texto:
Pocos episodios, una sola planta
El modelo se entrenó con **24 episodios** de etiqueta (20 sin los dudosos) de **una sola maceta**: unas 5.660 filas a 5 minutos. Las filas contiguas comparten etiqueta y están muy correlacionadas, así que el tamaño real de la muestra son los episodios, no las filas. Con tan pocos episodios cualquier número de exactitud tiene un margen grande (±0,05 de F1 por bootstrap) y no hay garantía de que valga para otra planta, otra maceta u otro sustrato.

El marchitamiento nocturno no se detecta
La regla **no cumple la condición de seguridad** que se había fijado (recall de `marchita` ≥ 0,9; dio 0,77). El caso que falla es el episodio 12: la noche del 19/10 Ruperto estaba marchito con la sonda en unos 1758 mV, por debajo del corte de 1940 mV, y la regla dijo `estresada`. De noche la planta puede caerse con el sustrato menos seco que de día, y una regla sólo sobre la sonda no lo ve.

titulo: Lo que Ruperto no sabe: limitaciones conocidas
texto:
El corte de 5,5 h puede ser el horario del observador
Las observaciones `saludable` después de los riegos del 07, 12 y 17/10 llegaron 5 o 6 horas después de regar, siempre a las 23:00 o 00:00. El corte de 5,5 h de la regla puede estar aprendiendo cuándo miraba la persona, no cuánto tarda la planta en recuperarse.

La sonda se corroe
La escala de la sonda resistiva se encogió de septiembre a octubre (marchito en ~2832 mV en septiembre y ~1758–1954 mV en octubre). Los umbrales de 1716 y 1940 mV son de la escala de octubre; si la sonda sigue corroyéndose, se van a correr. La calibración semanal seco/mojado que debía registrar esa deriva está pendiente.

Etiquetas dudosas
Cuatro episodios tienen etiquetas que no se sostienen solas y se dejaron afuera del entrenamiento: el 8 (marchito con el sustrato igual que saludable, de noche), el 9 (estresado con el sustrato en el rango de saludable), el 11 (propagada 16 días después y contradicha por la observación siguiente) y el 14 (estresado, una etiqueta arrastrada 25 h después de un riego sin que nadie la confirmara).

Huecos y sensores caídos
La serie tiene huecos (reinicios, cortes de luz y las dos semanas del 17/09 al 01/10) que **no se completan ni se interpolan**. **La placa no manda datos desde el 2026-10-29 a las 21:12 UTC**: mientras no se vuelva a enchufar, Ruperto sólo puede hablar de su pasado, no de cómo está ahora.

Otros sensores
- El termistor marca al revés (38 °C en una noche fría, 9 °C sobre el radiador): no sirve como temperatura.
- La luz no está calibrada en lux; de 19 a 22 h hay una lámpara (~1780 mV), así que "luz alta" no siempre es sol.
- El DHT11 tiene resolución de 1 °C y ±5 % de humedad.
- Las temperaturas de 26–36 °C del 15 y 16/09 **no son errores**: la maceta estuvo sobre un radiador.

titulo: Quién es Ruperto y cómo está armada su maceta
texto:
La planta
Ruperto es un lirio de paz (*Spathiphyllum*), una planta de interior de la familia de las aráceas. Vive en una maceta "inteligente" armada para un curso de inteligencia artificial: una placa ESP32 le mide el sustrato y el ambiente, un modelo que corre en la misma placa decide si está bien, y desde la Tarea 3 un chatbot de Telegram (este) habla en su nombre. Hay una sola maceta: los datos que en la base figuran como `maceta-01` y como `maceta-02` (del 03/10 al 18/10, por un error de identificador) son la misma planta.

Los sensores de la placa
La placa de sensores es una ESP32 DevKit enchufada a un cargador de pared. Cada cinco minutos lee:

- **Humedad del sustrato** con una sonda **resistiva** (dos electrodos enterrados). Se reporta en milivoltios (`suelo_mv`); más milivoltios quiere decir sustrato más seco.
- **Temperatura y humedad relativa del aire** con un DHT11 (resolución de 1 °C y ±5 % de humedad: es una referencia gruesa). Con esas dos se calcula el déficit de presión de vapor (VPD), que mide cuánto "tira" el aire del agua de las hojas.
- **Luz** con una fotorresistencia (LDR), en milivoltios (`luz_mv`). No está calibrada en lux; de noche, con oscuridad total, marca alrededor de 142 mV.
- Un **termistor** que no se usa: su conversión de temperatura quedó invertida en el firmware y marca frío cuando hace calor.

Cada lectura analógica es la mediana de 9 muestras. Si un sensor falla, el valor viaja vacío (no en cero) y el motivo queda anotado.

titulo: Quién es Ruperto y cómo está armada su maceta
texto:
El semáforo, el botón y la pantalla
La maceta tiene tres LEDs: **verde** = saludable, **amarillo** = estresado, **rojo** = marchito. Los prende el modelo que corre en la placa, no una persona. Si los tres están apagados es que no hay predicción (por ejemplo, porque el sensor de aire no dio datos desde el arranque).

El botón sirve para que una persona anote lo que ve: una pulsación corta cambia la "condición observada" que viaja con la medición (eso es la etiqueta para entrenar), y una pulsación larga fuerza un envío. Una pantalla LCD muestra las lecturas y la predicción.

A dónde van los datos
Cada medición viaja por HTTPS a un backend propio (FastAPI) y se guarda en una base Postgres en Railway, con la hora de la placa sincronizada por NTP en UTC. Una segunda placa, una ESP32-CAM independiente, saca una foto de la planta cada 5 minutos y la sube al mismo backend. Un panel web muestra la serie y el árbol de decisión del modelo.

Las tres clases
| clase del modelo | cómo lo dice Ruperto | qué significa en botánica |
|---|---|---|
| `saludable` | saludable | turgente: hojas firmes y erguidas |
| `estresada` | estresado | marchitez transitoria: empieza a perder turgencia, o se está recuperando de un riego |
| `marchita` | marchito | marchitez franca: hojas caídas, el "desmayo" típico del lirio de paz con sed |

Las clases van en femenino porque son los nombres internos del firmware y de los datos (se refieren a "la planta"); Ruperto es varón y habla de sí mismo en masculino.

Las etiquetas las puso una persona observando la planta y apretando el botón. Cuando nadie la miró, la etiqueta se arrastra desde la última observación y se marca como "propagada", que vale menos que una observación directa.

titulo: Cómo mide la sonda de suelo y por qué más mV es más seco
texto:
Una sonda resistiva
La humedad del sustrato se mide con una sonda **resistiva**: dos electrodos metálicos enterrados que forman, junto con una resistencia fija, un divisor de tensión. El agua del sustrato conduce la corriente. Con el sustrato mojado la resistencia entre los electrodos es baja y la tensión que lee la placa también; con el sustrato seco la resistencia es alta y la tensión sube.

Por eso **más milivoltios quiere decir más seco**: el valor "seco" de calibración es mayor que el "mojado". Un riego se ve como una caída brusca de `suelo_mv` (en octubre, de unos 1935 a unos 1500 mV en una sola muestra).

Por qué se alimenta sólo durante la lectura
Mientras hay tensión aplicada, los iones del agua migran hacia los electrodos (electrólisis): la lectura deriva hacia abajo y los electrodos se corroen. Para limitarlo, la sonda se alimenta desde un pin de la placa (GPIO 33) **sólo mientras se mide**, con una espera fija de 100 ms. Esa espera no se alarga: el divisor se asienta en microsegundos y lo que importa es que sea siempre la misma.

titulo: Cómo mide la sonda de suelo y por qué más mV es más seco
texto:
La corrosión y la deriva
Los electrodos se corroen con las semanas y la escala de la sonda se encoge: la misma humedad real se lee distinto en la semana 3 que en la semana 1. La mediana de `suelo_mv` en los episodios de marchitez franca fue de unos **2832 mV en septiembre**, **1954 mV del 03/10 al 18/10** y **1758 mV el 19/10**. Como la condición de la planta también cambia con el tiempo, esa deriva puede confundirse con una señal real; es el riesgo metodológico más serio del montaje.

La mitigación prevista es medir una vez por semana el par de referencia seco (sonda al aire) y mojado (sonda en un vaso de agua) y anotarlo en `docs/CALIBRACION.md`. Al 2026-11-03 esa tabla de calibración semanal sigue **pendiente**: no hay mediciones registradas.

Valores de referencia en octubre
Con la escala de octubre, del 03/10 al 18/10 el sustrato acompañó a la etiqueta en todos los episodios: saludable alrededor de 1500–1610 mV, estresado alrededor de 1840–1870 mV y marchito alrededor de 1940–1960 mV. Después de un riego baja a unos 1400–1520 mV.

`suelo_pct` (el porcentaje que muestra la pantalla) no está calibrado y no se usa para nada; el modelo usa `suelo_mv`.

El transitorio al arrancar
Cuando la placa arranca o se vuelve a meter la sonda en la tierra, la lectura arranca alta y baja de a poco durante decenas de minutos (una exponencial con constante de 24 a 83 minutos según el arranque). Por eso los primeros minutos después de un arranque no se usan para entrenar y no cuentan para detectar riegos. Si la sonda está fuera del sustrato, el ADC se satura (3124 mV) y esa lectura se trata como faltante.
